comparison: Both OpenEval and peer reviewers agree that the 14-3-3/spastin interaction data (C1, C40-C45) is convincing and well-supported. Peer reviewers explicitly state the binding partner data is solid. Complete agreement on biochemical interaction evidence.

Both evaluations support the phosphorylation-dependent regulation and mapping data (C46-C53). Peer reviewers explicitly accept the regulation by phosphorylation as convincing. OpenEval provides more detailed analysis of the mapping and isoform data, but both reach the same positive conclusion.

Perfect agreement on claims C2, C60-C72 regarding 14-3-3 protection of spastin from ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Both evaluations identify this as a major strength with solid evidence from CHX chase, proteasome inhibition, and ubiquitination assays.

Major disagreement on microtubule severing claims (C3, C73-C77). OpenEval finds the severing assay data supportive, while peer reviewers explicitly state 'the data to infer Spastin actions on Microtubules across different experimental models is weak' and that claims about MT severing were wrongly used.

OpenEval supports claims C54-C55 about S233 mutations retaining severing activity. Peer reviewers' general criticism of microtubule severing data interpretation applies here, creating uncertainty about these specific claims despite OpenEval's positive assessment.

Both evaluations support the neurite outgrowth data in hippocampal neurons (C57-C59). Peer reviewers implicitly accept this as part of solid cellular functional evidence, while OpenEval provides detailed analysis. Agreement on this in vitro functional data.

OpenEval supports the pharmacological tool data (C68-C69) showing FC-A and R18 effects on 14-3-3/spastin binding. Peer reviewers accept this data as part of the interaction evidence without specific criticism of these co-IP experiments.

Significant disagreement on FC-A neurite outgrowth/regeneration claims (C4, C78-C86). OpenEval finds strong mechanistic evidence, but peer reviewers raise major concerns about spastazoline selectivity, noting it 'has a major impact on neurite outgrowth' and questioning whether FC-A effects are specifically spastin-mediated versus reflecting general spastazoline toxicity.

Complete agreement on temporal expression patterns after SCI (C5, C87-C96). Both evaluations accept the western blot and immunofluorescence data showing 14-3-3 and spastin expression changes over time. Peer reviewers do not challenge this characterization.

Strong agreement on locomotor recovery data (C6, C110-C117). Both evaluations identify this as a major strength with solid behavioral and electrophysiological evidence. Peer reviewers explicitly state 'The finding that Fusicoccin (FC-A) promotes locomotor recovery after spinal cord injury is supported by solid data.'

Both address nerve regeneration claims (C6, C97-C98) but with different emphases. OpenEval focuses on histological evidence while peer reviewers emphasize the locomotor recovery aspect. Some overlap in claim coverage but different analytical focus.

Major disagreement on histological nerve regeneration evidence (C7, C99-C101, C120-C127). OpenEval finds the immunofluorescence data supportive, but peer reviewers explicitly state 'The histological data and analyses following spinal cord injury are not convincing' citing poor image quality and resolution insufficient to support quantitative claims.

Disagreement on acetylated tubulin data interpretation (C102-C108). OpenEval accepts this as evidence of microtubule dynamics changes, while peer reviewers state claims about 'microtubules dynamics' were wrongly used given the provided evidence. Challenges the mechanistic interpretation.

Both evaluations support the neural stem/progenitor cell proliferation data (C128-C131). OpenEval notes this suggests multiple mechanisms of action, and peer reviewers do not specifically challenge this finding despite criticizing other histological data.

Agreement on functional recovery in lateral hemisection model (C132-C137). Both evaluations accept this data as supporting FC-A effects on locomotor recovery. Peer reviewers include this as part of the solid locomotor recovery evidence.

Disagreement on acetylated tubulin mechanistic interpretation (C138-C140). OpenEval accepts this as confirming drug delivery and microtubule dynamics modulation, while peer reviewers challenge the inference about spastin actions on microtubules.

Partial disagreement on spastin-dependence conclusions (C8, C142). OpenEval finds spastazoline reversal experiments provide strong evidence for spastin-dependence, but peer reviewers note concerns about spastazoline selectivity and lack of direct evidence that 14-3-3 and spastin function as a complex in the same pathway to promote regeneration.

Disagreement on overall conclusions (C145, C167-C168). OpenEval finds the comprehensive evidence supports the main conclusions about 14-3-3 as a molecular switch and FC-A as therapeutic strategy. Peer reviewers accept some aspects (locomotor recovery, molecular interaction) but challenge others (histological evidence, microtubule dynamics interpretation, spastin-dependence specificity).
